items.confound_note: All four kilns sit at Kestrel inside Q1, so they share one production history. Throughput halved against the earlier quarter and every stack ran at reduced burner load, and burning half as much material lowers particulate on its own. Because each unit is compared against itself a quarter earlier rather than against an unupgraded unit in the same quarter, nothing in the log separates the filter upgrade from the slowdown.
items.notes: Cases must be byte-identical to coherent_true; only the closing sentence differs. Check that the slowdown works as a single cause covering all four cases at once, which it does only because all four kilns share site and quarter. Check the closer reuses the same vocabulary as the true closer (throughput, burner load, earlier quarter, every stack) so the contrast is logical rather than lexical.

items.confound_note: Every case measures backpressure across the filter housing, not particulate at the stack outlet. Backpressure records how loaded the media is, and freshly fitted media reads lower by construction; a split bag or a bypassing seal reads lower still while letting more particulate through. The claim is about particulate readings, so the four measurements taken on 26 February, 28 May, 27 August and 25 November do not bear on it.
items.notes: Closing sentence is verbatim identical to both TRUE items; the conditions and dates are verbatim identical to diverse_true. The only change is the measured-quantity word: particulate becomes backpressure. Check that backpressure is genuinely non-equivalent to a particulate reading (low backpressure can accompany higher emissions when media is torn or bypassed) and that this substitute wording is not reused by another family.
